source: CARDI (2011), "Series on: Rice Cultivation Environment Status in Cambodia / Soil Group Classification / Key Characteristics of 10 Rice Varieties / Simple Seed Purification Method" (Khmer, 25pp, funded by CAVAC/ACIAR, 1st printing 2011); CARDI (2011), "Handbook of Integrated Techniques for Increasing Wet-Season and Dry-Season Rice Productivity" (Khmer, 50pp, funded by CAVAC/ACIAR, foreword by H.E. Chan Sarun, Minister of Agriculture, dated 26 August 2011)
text: Cambodian rice land is grouped by CARDI into four main growing environments (ekasetr borisdthan, ẗកសេតបរិស្ឋាន) based on water source and standing-water depth. (1) Upland fields (srae kpoung leu) are well-drained, never hold standing water, and have no hardpan; farmers grow dryland/upland rice here, a rice with a deep, strongly branching root system that must draw water and nutrients from a dry profile. Upland area has stayed roughly stable around 25,000–28,000 ha nationally over recent years. (2) Rainfed lowland, bunded fields (srae tumnob rompeng teuk pnleang) hold standing rainwater for up to about one month, typically drying out in October; CARDI splits this into four sub-types by standing-water depth in the rainy season and drainage time after rain stops: Upper terrace (srae leu) — water depth 5–20 cm, drains in about 10 days; suited to early/non-photoperiod-sensitive short varieties (<120-day duration, 90–120 cm tall) such as Sen Pidor, Chol'sa and IR66, which flower before mid-October or mature 5–15 November. Area fell sharply from about 480,000 ha (2009) to 450,000–460,000 ha (2010). Middle terrace (srae kandal) — water depth 5–30 cm, drains in 15–20 days; suited to medium-duration photoperiod-sensitive varieties (120–150 cm tall) flowering 15 October–7 November or maturing 15 November–7 December, such as Phka Rumduol, Phka Rumdeng, Phka Romeat and Phka Chan Sen Sar; this is also the best zone for premium/fragrant grain quality. Area grew from about 1.8 million ha (2009) to over 2.1–2.2 million ha (2010). Lower terrace (srae kraom) — water depth 5–50 cm, drains from about 30 days; suited to heavy/long-duration photoperiod-sensitive varieties (130–170 cm tall) flowering 8 November–15 December, such as Roeung Chey, Khor 4 and Khor 6. Area fell from about 520,000–527,000 ha (2009) to 490,000–495,000 ha (2010). Early-wet-season/pre-season rice (srae daeum rodov vossa) — grown only where farmers have a supplemental irrigation source (reservoir, pond, or shallow groundwater) to plant one early crop before the main wet-season crop; feasible only on middle- and lower-terrace land because those zones retain enough water to support both crops; uses short-duration, non-photoperiod-sensitive varieties (≤120 days) such as Sen Pidor, Chol'sa and IR66. (3) Deepwater environment (ekasetr borisdthan teuk chrew) holds standing water from about 50 cm up to 4 m deep in the rainy season, draining only after 40+ days; split into floating rice (water up to 2.5 m) and deepwater rice proper (water beyond 2.5 m). Area was small and grew from about 1,000 ha (2009) to roughly 9,000–9,600 ha (2010). (4) Dry-season/irrigated environment (ekasetr borisdthan srae pramang) depends wholly or mostly on irrigation rather than rainfall, and uses non-photoperiod-sensitive short varieties (Sen Pidor, Chol'sa, IR66); it is split into three sub-types: fully irrigated dry-season rice (srae raksrouk, water supplied from an irrigation system, reservoir or groundwater from sowing to maturity), flood-recession rice grown along the edge of large lakes/water bodies chasing the receding water level with supplemental irrigation (srae bordeanh teuk), and pre-flood-season rice grown along lake/water-body edges to be harvested before the flood arrives, using irrigation plus rainfall (srae mun teuk chol). Dry-season area grew from about 380,000–384,000 ha (2009) to 450,000 ha (2010).
caveat: This 4-environment / sub-type framework and its area figures (2009 vs 2010, in hectares) come from two CARDI 2011 publications and very likely overlaps with 'ecosystem type' content already in the KB from earlier batches (flagged there as an open duplicate-check item, and also relevant to the standing three-way transplanting-spacing discrepancy and flood-zone variety table open items). The area figures are a 2009/2010 snapshot only, not current. Variety names given here (e.g. 'Chol'sa') are transcribed from OCR of a scanned, encrypted, non-Limon-font PDF and should be checked against known KB variety spellings (this may be the same variety flagged elsewhere as an unresolved 'Cholmol/Chulsa' identity item).
